title: Training data and copyright: still unsettled

sources.claim: US Copyright Office, Part 3: Generative AI Training (pre-publication version, May 9, 2025): whether training on copyrighted works is fair use depends on the facts; uses that produce outputs competing with the originals weigh against fair use. An agency report is not binding law.

In June 2025 two federal district judges in California (Bartz v. Anthropic; Kadrey v. Meta) found that training on the books at issue was fair use on those records, while treating pirated copies differently (Bartz) or warning that other evidence could change the result (Kadrey). District-court rulings are fact-specific and do not settle the question nationwide.

jurisdiction: US federal (agency report); US federal (district courts, California)

questions.intro: Whether training AI on COPYRIGHTED WORKS without permission is legal is STILL UNSETTLED in the United States. A key question is FAIR USE, a legal doctrine weighing purpose, the nature of the work, how much was used, and the effect on the market. In June 2025, two federal district judges in California (Bartz v. Anthropic; Kadrey v. Meta) found training on the books at issue was fair use on those records, with important limits. The US Copyright Office's May 2025 report said the answer depends on the facts. Many other cases are pending.

sections.skill: Read rulings and reports with care

questions.prompt: Do district-court rulings bind other courts nationwide?

choices.text: Yes, every district-court ruling must be followed by every other court in the country

questions.intro: Reading these developments carefully matters. District-court rulings are fact-specific and do not bind other courts nationwide; appeals can change outcomes. In Bartz, pirated copies were treated differently from lawfully obtained books; in Kadrey, the judge warned that different evidence about market harm could change the result. The Copyright Office report is guidance, not binding law. So the accurate summary is: open, contested and changing.

questions.prompt: In Bartz, how were pirated copies treated?
